article_text:
The Jan van Eyck Academie in the Netherlands, invites artists, designers, curators, writers, architects and artistic researchers worldwide to apply for its eleven-month residency programme, offering studio facilities, accommodation, financial support and opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration.

Open Call:

The Jan van Eyck Academie has opened applications for its 2028 residency programme, inviting international practitioners from diverse artistic and research disciplines to develop their work within a collaborative environment in Maastricht, the Netherlands. Running from 15 January to 15 December 2028, the programme welcomes individual practitioners, duos and collectives, including applicants with children. Approximately 30 to 32 participants will be selected through the general open call, joining a wider cohort of around 36 residents. The residency supports both material-based and research-driven practices, encouraging participants to investigate contemporary social, environmental and cultural questions alongside more personal artistic enquiries. Through access to specialist facilities, professional guidance and peer exchange, participants are encouraged to experiment, collaborate and expand their creative practices.

Institutional Context:

The Jan van Eyck Academie is an international post-academic institute for art, design and reflection based in Maastricht, the Netherlands. The institution supports artistic research and experimentation across disciplines, giving participants opportunities to develop their practices through critical dialogue, collaborative research, and material exploration. Residents have access to the academy’s specialist laboratories, including Photography & Audiovisual, Material Matters, Food, Printing & Publishing, and Future Materials. Advisers, the curator and resident liaison, the departments of Nature Research and Education & Development, and the academy’s library also provide support. The programme encourages participants to engage with institutional public programmes, where artistic experimentation intersects with contemporary social and environmental debates.

Eligibility and Criteria:

Applications are open internationally to practitioners working across a broad range of disciplines, including:

Visual arts and interdisciplinary artistic practice.

Graphic, fashion, food and social design.

Architecture and spatial practice.

Curatorial practice.

Writing and artistic research.

Other experimental and research-driven creative disciplines.

Individual practitioners, duos, collectives and applicants with children are eligible. Applicants must demonstrate sufficient English proficiency to communicate and collaborate with fellow residents and staff. Dutch and English are the academy’s principal working languages.

Successful applicants must reside in Maastricht throughout the residency and register with the local municipality. Applicants previously enrolled as full-time participants at the Rijksakademie or De Ateliers in the Netherlands are not eligible.

The Jan van Eyck Academie is not a degree-awarding educational institution and does not provide academic credits or certificates.

Evaluation Process:

A selection committee comprising the Jan van Eyck director and five external arts professionals representing different areas of expertise will assess applications.

The committee will consider:

The applicant’s motivation for undertaking a residency at this stage of their artistic development.

The urgency, purpose and objectives of the proposed project.

The applicant’s capacity for critical thinking and reflection.

The relationship between the applicant’s practice, other artistic perspectives and wider contemporary concerns.

The final selection will also consider diversity across artistic disciplines, geographical backgrounds and gender.

Practical Information:

Application deadline: 1 December 2026, 23:59 CET

Residency dates: 15 January to 15 December 2028

Duration: Eleven months

Location: Jan van Eyck Academie, Maastricht, the Netherlands

Available places: Approximately 30 to 32 through the general call

Financial and practical support includes:

A monthly stipend of €1,500, from which accommodation rental and service costs are deducted.

A monthly stipend of €2,000 for participants with children, also subject to accommodation deductions.

A furnished private studio apartment for each participant.

Larger accommodation for participants with children and, where relevant, their partners.

Access to specialist laboratories, research facilities and professional guidance.

Visa application assistance where required.

Each member of an accepted duo receives an individual monthly stipend of €1,500 and a private studio apartment.

Fees:

Application fee: €65 excluding VAT, or €78.65 including VAT.

Enrolment fee for selected participants: €2,750 excluding VAT.

The application fee is waived for applicants who are both from and living in countries or territories classified as Least Developed, Low Income or Lower Middle Income on the OECD Development Assistance Committee’s list of official development assistance recipients.

Applications and Queries:

Submit applications online through the Jan van Eyck Academie’s Dapple application platform by 1 December 2026 at 23:59 CET .

Applicants must create an account and provide the following information in English:

Artist statement: Maximum 250 words or 1,400 characters.

Motivation: Maximum 500 words or 3,150 characters.

Project proposal: Maximum 500 words or 3,150 characters.

Portfolio: Documentation of recent work completed within the past five years, maximum 25 pages.

Curriculum vitae: Maximum two pages.

The portfolio and CV must be combined into a single PDF file of no more than 10 MB.

Alternatively, applicants may submit a video or audio recording of up to eight minutes addressing the artist statement, motivation and project proposal.

Duos and collectives must submit one joint application and pay only one application fee.

Applications cannot be modified after submission.

Official open call and application information: https://www.janvaneyck.nl/calendar/apply-now-jve-residency-2028

Enquiries: application@janvaneyck.nl

Telephone: +31 (0)43 350 37 09 or +31 (0)43 350 37 36

article_text:
A team of researchers at the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) in Mexico recently announced the discovery of a 2,500-year-old structure that they believe functioned as a solar observatory.

The structure is part of the pre-Hispanic Teteles de Ávila Castillo archaeological site in Sierra Norte de Puebla and has been under excavation by INAH since 2015. Alberto Diez Barroso Repizo, Teteles’s archaeological project director, told the Art Newspaper that Teteles “flourished during the Middle Preclassic period (900BC-600BC) but declined around AD100, possibly because nearby Cantona expanded.” Diez points to the discovery of green obsidian beads as an indication that Teteles, which is along a trade route, was connected to the much larger Mesoamerican city Teotihuacan, since that city controlled a quarry where the obsidian originated.

The discovery indicates that Teteles’s architects and inhabitants had a sophisticated knowledge of astronomy: the observatory was designed to track the beginning of the Mesoamerican calendar in February and the harvest in October, according to a statement from INAH. One of the project’s researchers noted that the eastern base of the complex “constitutes a solar calendar,” based on observations of the trajectory of the sun aligning with the front of the structure during the beginning of equinoxes and solstices.

Diez told TAN that INAH plans to open the site, and eventually a museum, to the public.

Claudia Curiel de Icaza, Mexico’s Secretary of Culture, noted that the discovery expands the country’s understanding of its own history. “The architecture of Teteles de Ávila Castillo tells us about societies that developed astronomical knowledge and incorporated it into the organization of their ceremonial spaces,” she said.

article_text:
Challenging the Eurocentric narratives of art history, ‘Along the Color Line: Traces of a Transatlantic Modernism’ at Museum Ludwig reveals the overlooked contributions of Black artists to modernism and the cultural exchanges that shaped artistic expression across continents.

Whose histories have been excluded from the story of modern art?

Marking Museum Ludwig’s 50th anniversary, ‘Along the Color Line: Traces of a Transatlantic Modernism’ examines the artistic and intellectual exchanges between the Black diaspora and European modernism, challenging established narratives of twentieth-century art. Curated by Eboa Itondo, the exhibition brings together painting, sculpture, drawing, literature and music, tracing connections between the Harlem Renaissance, the Négritude movement and contemporary artistic practices.

Taking its title from the writings of W. E. B. Du Bois, the exhibition considers how Black artists navigated racism, colonialism and cultural displacement while developing new visual languages and forms of representation. Works by Mildred Thompson, Herbert Gentry and Iba Ndiaye illuminate transatlantic artistic networks, while James Gregory Atkinson’s archival practice connects historical experiences of Black communities in Germany with contemporary questions of identity and belonging. By confronting the historical absence of Black artists within European museum collections, ‘Along the Color Line ’ invites audiences to reconsider who shaped modernism, whose contributions have been overlooked and how art history might be understood through a more interconnected global perspective.

This exhibition is on view at Museum Ludwig in Cologne until 7 March 2027

article_text:
Londra continua a correre. Dopo i risultati scoppiettanti di Christie’s , arriva anche la prova di forza di Sotheby’s: l’asta serale di Contemporary Art totalizza 46 milioni di sterline, pari a 61 milioni di dollari, confermando il momento positivo delle vendite nella capitale britannica. Ma il dato che fa davvero rumore è quello complessivo: dall’inizio dell’anno, le aste di arte moderna e contemporanea di Sotheby’s a Londra hanno raggiunto 598 milioni di sterline, circa 793 milioni di dollari, vale a dire il totale più alto per questo periodo dell’anno dal 2015. Considerando tutte le categorie, le vendite della casa d’aste nella capitale hanno inoltre superato il miliardo di dollari.

Quindi, i numeri della serata. A prendersi la scena da Sotheby’s Londra è stato Willem de Kooning: la sua Untitled del 1977 è stata venduta per 9,8 milioni di sterline, pari a 12,9 milioni di dollari, superando la soglia degli 8 milioni e raggiungendo un primato storico. È infatti il prezzo più alto mai pagato in un’asta europea per un’opera dell’artista. Un risultato che, da solo, dà la misura del peso dei grandi nomi nella vendita londinese.

Alle spalle di De Kooning si è piazzato Gerhard Richter, con il monumentale Abstraktes Bild del 1992, aggiudicato per 6,7 milioni di sterline, equivalenti a 8,9 milioni di dollari. Terzo risultato della serata per Mark Rothko: un Untitled su carta, realizzato nello stesso periodo dei celebri dipinti per la Rothko Chapel, ha raggiunto 3,8 milioni di sterline, pari a 5 milioni di dollari. Tre risultati che confermano la forza della domanda per l’astrazione e per alcuni dei protagonisti assoluti dell’arte del secondo Novecento.

Buona prova anche per David Hockney, il cui Henry Reading ha raggiunto 2,8 milioni di sterline, toccando il limite superiore della stima. Ancora più sorprendente, in rapporto alle aspettative, la performance di 10th – 22nd June 2021, Water Lilies in the Pond with Pots of Flowers : il lavoro è stato venduto da Sotheby’s Londra per 1,9 milioni di sterline, quasi tre volte la stima massima di 650.000 sterline. Un nuovo record d’asta per l’artista, per un’opera realizzata su iPad.

Sul fronte della Pop Art, Four Marilyns (Reversal Series) di Andy Warhol ha totalizzato 2,7 milioni di sterline, mentre il suo Portrait of Johann Wolfgang Von Goethe è stato aggiudicato per 1,5 milioni. L’arte tedesca ha dato un contributo significativo alla serata, a partire da Georg Baselitz. P.D. Idol ha raggiunto 2,4 milioni di sterline, superando la stima massima di 2 milioni, mentre Die Geißelung è stato venduto per 2,2 milioni. Anche Albert Oehlen ha centrato un risultato significativo: Schwindel , al suo debutto in asta, ha totalizzato 1,7 milioni di sterline, all’interno della forchetta di stima. I risultati arrivano dopo la vendita di Modern British & Irish Art organizzata dalla stessa Sotheby’s il giorno precedente, che aveva totalizzato 11,6 milioni di sterline, pari a 15,4 milioni di dollari. E il calendario non si ferma qui: sono in programma le aste diurne di Contemporary Art e la vendita dedicata a David Hockney.

«Questi risultati, che portano il nostro totale annuale a Londra oltre il miliardo di dollari, testimoniano la nostra fiducia nella città durante tutto l’anno», ha dichiarato Alex Branczik, presidente di Modern and Contemporary Art per Europa e Asia di Sotheby’s. La strategia della casa d’aste, ha sottolineato, va ben oltre una singola settimana di eventi e punta a mantenere Londra al centro del mercato globale dell’arte. Il messaggio è chiaro: con 46 milioni di sterline raccolti nella vendita serale, un totale annuale di 598 milioni per Moderno e Contemporaneo e un De Kooning che stabilisce un primato europeo, Sotheby’s mette a segno una serata di peso. Dopo Christie’s, un altro segnale importante per il mercato londinese, dove i grandi nomi continuano a catalizzare l’attenzione dei collezionisti internazionali. Ora si guarda a Parigi.

Films and events

Documentary Competition

Concrete Turned to Sand

Shaped by the tidal rhythms of British Columbia’s oyster farms, this richly cinematic documentary, shot on 35mm, exists where labour, scientific inquiry and the living world meet.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriters Jessica Johnson, Ryan Ermacora

Canada 2026. 73min

Courtesy of Slag Pile Films Ltd

Language English

Access information

Tuesday 13 October 14:15

Closed Captions (CC) via WatchWord smart glasses

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Shimmering underwater images of shellfish suspended in shifting currents and spectral nocturnal scenes lend this film an almost otherworldly beauty, as though moments from science fiction had surfaced within everyday life. With a contemplative rhythm and patient gaze, Jessica Johnson and Ryan Ermacora expand our perception of space and time, gently unsettling familiar ways of seeing and revealing the hidden transformations of the landscape.

Hyun Jin Cho

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

To Hold a Mountain

Set in the remote highlands of Montenegro, this year’s Sundance World Documentary Prize winner reflects on the fragile coexistence between ancestral knowledge and the growing pressures of the contemporary world.

Forest High

In this visually arresting film, solo caretakers keep the fires burning in a remote Alpine chalet where weary hikers find modest lodgings.

Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff

This awe-inspiring documentary is a detailed and thought-provoking portrait of the astronomer and astrophysicist behind Cosmos and Contact.

article_text:
Among the most staggering, unforgettable experiences one can have in a theater this year is Sandra Wollner’s Everytime , a drama about loss that skirts seemingly every convention one might want to pre-emptively box it into. Impeccably shot by Aftersun DP Gregory Oke, the Un Certain Regard winner, three-time Gotham Award nominee, and German Oscar entry will now get a one-week, awards-qualifying run beginning next week at NYC’s Film at Lincoln Center ahead of a February 12 release. In advance of the roll-out, 1-2 Special has now debuted the first teaser.

Here’s the synopsis: “On the eve of a family vacation, a shocking tragedy disrupts the lives of Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her younger daughter Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and their teenage family friend Lux (Tristan Lopez). One year later, after drifting in a state of suspended grief, the trio reunite and embark on a trip to Tenerife, hoping to recreate the family holiday that never happened. Under a strange new sun, they find that the past, present, and future begin to overlap.”

Rory O’Connor said in his Cannes review , “In Everytime , a sun-dappled film about death and love that might be the best in Cannes this year, the terrible loss of a teenage girl’s life leaves her mother, younger sister, and boyfriend bound in mutual devastation. Set in present-day East Berlin during the balmy months of the year, this is a film that appears at first to be drawn from the same Berlin School approach as Christian Petzold and Angela Schanelec, but there’s little of that cohort’s minimalism or literary melancholy here. No need to know that the DP is Gregory Oke for one’s mind to gradually wander to Charlotte Wells’ Aftersun —another movie about how the worst things still manage to happen regardless of the weather.”

article_text:
P aul Greengrass has in fact already made his “uprising” film: United 93 , the gut-wrenching 2006 masterpiece about the passengers onboard United Airlines flight 93 who rose up against the 9/11 hijackers and prevented them from hitting their destination and causing fatalities – except, that is, for those onboard the plane. Greengrass’s new movie, shot in his distinctive handheld, docu-reportage style, is notionally about the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, in which Wat Tyler and John Ball became legendary for leading an insurrection against the cruel poll tax of Richard II. Or at least … it sort of is. Because the film, in a disconcertingly silly way, imagines the uprising as an origin myth for Robin Hood, or at least someone who’s supposed to be more or less Robin Hood – because that’s not what he’s called and the dates don’t quite match up.

Ex-soldier Tyler and radical preacher Ball, capably played by Cosmo Jarvis and Jamie Bell, are joined by a third fictional hero, apparently destined later to canter through the forest with a wealth-redistribution plan. He is a ploughman, known simply as “Ploughman”, played by Andrew Garfield; grieving the loss of his wife and children to the plague and sickened by the tax collectors’ greed and brutality, he instigates an insurrection that soon merges into other outbreaks of revolutionary rage. This involves rivers of smudgy-faced folk in rough clothes descending on the capital from all directions, to demand concessions from the king to whom they are still loyal and believe to have been misled by advisers.

The appearance of the well-bathed royal overlords themselves may remind you of the immortal line from Monty Python and the Holy Grail about how to tell if someone is a king. Tom Hollander gives a very enjoyable performance as his majesty’s evil adviser Sir Robert Hales, and Katherine Waterston is typically stylish and composed as Joan of Kent, the king’s mother, while Woody Norman has a sinister moon-faced blankness as the young Richard II himself. There are moments to enjoy in all the overclass performances, and indeed to respect in those of the doomed uprisers, whose heroism nonetheless is supposed to create a historic legacy of fighting against bullies and tyrants.

That, it seems, is the point of it all. Which brings us to the coda; I wondered if Greengrass would boldly hit us with an immersive scene from London’s 1990 poll tax riots. But no. It’s Garfield emerging from the dense forest with his un-merry men like a gag-free episode of Blackadder, and being oddly lenient with the ermine-clad VIPs that they catch. It’s a bit of letdown.

article_text:
Photographer and filmmaker Neal Slavin returns to his alma mater for a conversation with artist and author M. Leona Godin . Their conversation will explore perception and what it truly means to see.

Neal Slavin met M. Leona Godin at the New York Public Library, where Godin was the 2025–26 Jean Strouse Fellow in the Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers. As a fellow, Godin was working on a book about blindness, photography, and image description. Their first encounter sparked many long conversations on the ways perception shapes how we experience the world through photography.

This evening’s conversation will explore the phenomenon of synesthesia, where the boundaries among the senses dissolve and the languages of music, poetry, painting, and photography intermingle. Together, they will discuss how perception moves beyond eyesight alone, and how photography continues to expand our understanding of what it means to see.

Slavin’s portraits have been published in several books, including Portugal , Britons , and When Two or More Are Gathered Together , recently republished and expanded with new photographs that bring together portraits taken over a span of 50 years (1974–2023). He was the recipient of a Fulbright Fellowship in Photography and of Cooper Union’s highest honor, the President’s Citation. Slavin’s photographs are in numerous permanent collections, including The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Centre Pompidou, and the New York Public Library, where Godin first encountered his work.

M. Leona Godin is a blind writer, artist, and the author of There Plant Eyes: A Personal and Cultural History of Blindness . She is currently working on a project about photography, blindness, and what it means to see, which received recent support from an NYPL Cullman Center Fellowship.

article_text:
Tina Barney’s mother, Lillian Fox, was five foot two and from Brooklyn, yet she made her name in New York as a fashion model in the 1930s. She started out as a face on point-of-sale advertising for Gillette razor blades and as an ambassador for Kayser hosiery: “Miss Lillian Fox writes, ‘Kayser’s new Bon Voyage hosiery colors do such exciting things to my Spring clothes, it’s hard to choose from the grand array.’” Yet her proficiency as a model—her facial beauty, and the way she wore a hat—gained her work in high-end fashion magazines, notably Harper’s Bazaar and Vogue .

Fox was shot by émigré fashion photographers George Hoyningen-Huene and Horst P. Horst, who recast the props of European civilization—the classical pillar, the Louis XV gilt chair—as symbols of American refinement. In a Horst photograph published in the March 1940 issue of Vogue , Fox models an elaborately cut evening cape in contrasting green and purple silk panels by American fashion designer Charles James. Olga Tritt jewelry snakes around her wrist and ear, echoing the rococo plaster swirl of the backdrop.

In another shot by Horst of four models arranged around a table laid in impeccable white linen, Fox sits furthest right while New York socialite Babe Paley inspects an oversized hat pin using a magnifying glass. Her exacting, almost imperious expression crystallizes the attention paid to designed goods in expressing elite American taste in the postwar era: a shaken cocktail of WASP understatement and meritocratic agency.

It was a world that Tina Barney was born to. From childhood, she was surrounded by art—her father’s family were collectors—and by the well-dressed, elegant women of her parents’ social circle. The family home bore her mother’s taste (Fox had a second career as an interior designer). As Barney recalls, “the interiors I grew up in were extraordinary in themselves.”

The young family appeared in Vogue, in 1949, on holiday in Long Island, and media attention followed Barney into married life. She and her family lived the American “good life,” roving the Upper East Side and the Rhode Island coastline. They exuded social poise and good dress sense at a time when fashion was becoming a reportable aspect of society life. By the 1960s, publisher John Fairchild had transformed the New York trade journal Women’s Wear Daily into WWD , a paper that covered the women who wore the clothes as much as the designers who made them. In 1968, WWD reported on a family party to which Barney wore “Oscar de la Renta’s short raspberry silver-beaded dress that’s been turning up at all the best parties this season.” Her sister Jill regularly appeared in The New York Times , dressed in the latest fashions, photographed by Bill Cunningham.

Tina Barney: Fashion

Part memoir, part survey, Tina Barney: Fashion explores style and sartorial expression across the celebrated portraitist’s career.

Barney had studied art history as a teenager, but her interest in photography grew while she was married with two children. It started in 1972 when she worked as a volunteer in MoMA’s Department of Photography; a year later Barney relocated with her family from New York to Sun Valley, Idaho, where she enrolled at Sun Valley Center for the Arts (now Sun Valley Museum of Art) to study photography.

From the late 1970s, Barney used her extended family and their surroundings as the subject matter for her large-format color photographs. The resulting images were arrangements of domestic life, planned with the object-oriented symbolism of some of the art she was surrounded by, or according to the remembered words of her mother: “You should have different heights of furniture in your room to excite the eye.”

By 1987, as her work became better exhibited, her New York gallerist Janet Borden suggested Barney should accept a fashion editorial commission from Connoisseur magazine, the British art periodical for collectors that had been reinvented as a full-color Hearst magazine run from New York. Overseen by the former Metropolitan Museum of Art director Thomas Hoving, Connoisseur expanded its remit to the broader expression of taste. In his column My Eye , in the March 1988 issue, Hoving described that the magazine had “moved beyond the restricted world of art and antiques into a complex range of subjects. We suspected that our readers wanted to know about the best of everything.”

Barney’s front-page editorial in the same issue introduced the menswear of Japanese fashion designer Issey Miyake. Though the interview had been conducted in Miyake’s design studio in Tokyo, Barney shot her family and friends wearing his clothes at home in Rhode Island and New York. In one picture, Barney’s son and his friends sport Miyake raincoats over neoprene wetsuits and deck shoes, standing on a town dock as if about to clamber aboard a boat.

While the clothes are conceptually and technically rigorous—the man on the cover wears a white linen suit, its shawl collar described by the seams of the jacket; the lilac bowtie at his neck is cast silicone—they are presented with a bodily ease that makes the wearer look rich, relaxed, and most important of all, socially acceptable in an elite world. While this is the masterstroke of the editorial, Barney’s motivation lay elsewhere: “We were supposed to be advertising Miyake—but basically, I really did whatever I wanted to do. I wasn’t thinking about the clothes. Funnily enough, I was thinking about just making a good picture. I wasn’t really informed enough about Miyake’s clothes, I must say. But I think it was a different thing to do.” Up to this moment, Miyake’s advertising campaigns had been shot by Irving Penn, who made the garments look like abstract sculpture first, clothes second. Seen against this sanctioned, intellectual approach, Barney’s editorial was truly radical.

Her commercial work garnered further fashion commissions, brokered by her long-term agent, Norma Jean Markus. To date, Barney has produced campaigns for Dior, Self-Portrait, Gucci, Thom Browne, and Tory Burch, and for fashion magazines, including Arena Homme Plus , L’Officiel , POP , Vogue , and Vogue Italia . She remains best known, however, for her fashion work for W magazine.

W began as a bimonthly sister magazine to WWD in 1972, and in 1993 it was relaunched as a large-format, monthly fashion title with Dennis Freedman as creative director. Freedman set out to improve the quality of the magazine’s photography, and he began by commissioning a mix of established fine-art and emerging fashion photographers who took the kind of pictures in which you might not notice the clothes. Freedman offered image makers such as Philip-Lorca diCorcia, Larry Fink, Craig McDean, Martin Parr, Juergen Teller, Larry Sultan, and Bruce Weber carte blanche. He allowed them to retain control of the selection of images and guaranteed their photographs would be published uncropped and printed with high-quality ink on large-format, glossy paper. When he asked Barney if she might consider a commission, she had one condition: “I need to have interesting people who live in interesting locations.”

For the resulting editorial, “New York Stories,” published in October 1999, Barney took her usual approach to fashion pictures, but made it strange by photographing families that were not her own: the mother sitting on the stairs with her child is Julianne Moore; the mature woman lost in contemplation in her apartment is Joan Didion.

Freedman has openly spoken about the creative constraints of fashion pictures, of the inevitable tension between artistic ideals and commercial requirements. Yet he has also used the example of this editorial, in particular the image of the art dealer Angela Westwater’s family—dressed in black by Ralph Lauren—to demonstrate how the parameters of an assignment can, counterintuitively, add an element of the unexpected: “If this were one of Tina’s personal works, the Westwaters would have chosen their own clothes and the result would have been very different, but not necessarily ‘better.’” In Barney’s hands, the picture is about the unease of the group. The fashion adds the surprising air of a funeral gathering.

Many of the acclaimed W portfolios by art and fashion photographers went on to be exhibited, sold as editioned photographs, and published in book form. In their repurposed formats, they were stripped of the original context of the magazine issue. Barney’s “New York Stories,” for example, was produced for an issue dedicated to American society, from profiles of the Astors and von Furstenbergs, to coverage of guests at the launch of Tina Brown’s Talk magazine; from an excerpt of Vanity Fair reporter Dominick Dunne’s Hollywood memoir, to a feature on the magazine’s best pre-millennium party photographs. In context, “New York Stories” is a pictorial fable about a kind of über family—successful in all arenas, dynastic, dysfunctional, performing ordinary life in extraordinary outfits.

In 1988, Barney coproduced a short documentary about Horst P. Horst directed by Mark Trottenberg. In the documentary, Horst reflects that “early on there were no such thing as models. They were just people that you knew, or that turned up somewhere or other.” It might be Barney describing her relatives and friends.

In the late 1950s, Horst was commissioned by Vogue to photograph the homes and gardens of notable people with exquisite style for a Fashions in Living column. The first, in 1957, was “the special triumph of Christian Dior’s Paris house.” These formal interiors, informally framed, were eventually published as Vogue’s Book of Houses, Gardens, People . On the book’s cover is a portrait of Mariga Guinness, the former Princess Hermione Marie-Gabrielle von Urach, at home in Leixlip Castle, in County Kildare, Ireland. She sits uneasily on a Georgian stool, up against the swagged valance of her dressing table, which almost buckles under an excessive floral arrangement. With her silver vanity set lying precariously at the edge of the table by her resting arm, she seems to wonder at the very idea of getting ready in front of such a thing. Carefully composed, the photograph also permits a glimpse beyond the mystique, revealing the sacrifice and cost that must be borne in keeping up appearances.

Horst’s photographs conjure la belle vie , the comfort and pleasure in being held in one’s environment, embodied as elegance. Horst was particular about his own definition of the term: “The most I can confidently say is that elegance is a way of making the best of one’s body without showing off, a way of feeling naturally at ease with one’s shape and stance and clothes and surroundings.” Horst might be describing Lillian Fox as depicted in one of his photographs, or equally, the artistry of Tina Barney.

Barney is a photographer with a deep fashion lineage. Her position is not that of the dispassionate observer; rather, it is formed from an understanding of a life lived camera-ready. Her fashion pictures materialize her maternal inheritance—that living well is the best revenge.

article_text:
A booksellers’ prize for photography books, awarded by booksellers France PhotoBook, an association of leading French publishers of photography books, is delighted to announce the fourth edition of the Booksellers’ Prize for Photography Books!

For its fourth edition, the Booksellers’ Prize brings together a jury of fifteen booksellers from across France. Their task is to select a winning book from among 24 titles published during the 2025–2026 academic year by France PhotoBook’s member publishers. The prize, worth €3,000, is awarded to the photographer. The publisher of the winning book also receives support to promote the work, by organising bookshop events. The prize is awarded thanks to the support of the Académie des Beaux-Arts, Pollen Diffusion and the MEP – Maison européenne de la photographie. The jury for this fourth edition is chaired by the writer Maylis de Kerangal. A shortlist of ten titles will be presented in September. A list of five finalists will be announced in early October, ahead of the announcement of the winner on 19 October 2026.

article_text:
“Desert Chant,” the first single from “ Dune: Part Three ” has been released.

The single begins with Timothée Chalamet humming before ascending into the war chant. The track is written by composer Hans Zimmer , who also scored the previous films.

“Dune: Part Three” sees Chalamet return as Paul Atreides, continuing the story after his ascent to power at the end of “Part Two.” Inspired by Frank Herbert’s novel “Dune Messiah,” the action takes place 17 years after the events of the previous film and explores the consequences of Paul’s rule as emperor. And things are getting…dark. Really, really dark. As lovers of the first film know, Paul is blessed with visions of the future, but his mind has grown clouded since assuming control of the galaxy.

For Zimmer, returning to Arrakis meant returning to the book that first lit his imagination as a teenager, the same book that, years later, would bond him with Villeneuve.

Zimmer says, “When two teenagers are deeply moved by the same novel that lets their imagination run wild, so wild that the mysticism and philosophy that captured their souls never lets them go, they will inevitably meet and become creative brothers.” He adds, “For me, the beauty of working on ‘Dune’ was that it would take me back into a time of being full of youthful imagination, where everything was true and the impossible was possible. I truly believe that Denis and I never stopped dreaming those dreams the book lit like fire in us teenagers, but now we had learned the craft and knowledge, having done a few films, to turn our mental images into reality.”

Returning cast members include Rebecca Ferguson, Javier Bardem and Pugh, whose role as Princess Irulan expands in the new film. Anya Taylor-Joy also reprises her role as Alia Atreides, who becomes a devoted follower of her brother. New additions to the cast include not only Pattinson but also Isaach de Bankolé as Paul’s former Fedaykin death commando.

“Dune: Part Three” debuts in theaters on Dec. 18.

Kering Women in Motion , an allied program of the Tokyo International Film Festival , held a talk event on Tuesday at Toho Cinemas Roppongi Hills for a packed crowd.

Director Kore-eda Hirokazu (“Shoplifters”) opened the event with brief remarks. “In recent years, I’ve been hearing people at international film festivals say, ‘Japanese films are really interesting right now.’ That’s a sentiment we didn’t hear 10 years ago,” he said. “Led by Hamaguchi Ryusuke and Fukada Koji, directors in their 20s and 30s have been taking their works overseas, and through their accumulated efforts and recognition, the attention given to Japanese films has been increasing. How to pass this on to the next generation and spread it further is a challenge for the older generation, and I think it’s also very important for film fans who are exposed to these works.”

National cinemas also exist parallel to each other, she added, but “that does not make one more important or one more harder than the other,” she said. “American film history is just as important as Japanese film history and just as important as French film history.”

By taking a broad view of film history and experiencing different types of cinema, she said, “We allow ourselves to learn so much more about a lived experience that’s outside of our own, because there’s no better way to develop empathy to develop cultural understanding than through watching a movie.”

Murata, the producer of the 2025 smash-hit kabuki-themed drama “Kokuho,” which received rave reviews abroad and was nominated for a Best Makeup and Hairstyling Oscar, said she wanted to “create something that will move as many people as possible, make as many people laugh as possible, and make as many people cry as possible.”

For that to happen, she added, tolerance of varying cultural perspectives is essential. “The worst case is a world in which that becomes difficult,” she said.

Homma commented that as a museum director in charge of various teams doing everything from research to marketing, “It’s always about who the best person would be.” Her aim, she added, was “for many people to bring their own cultural differences or their own unique qualities and have that be seen as a strength. I don’t want anyone to shy or hide their individualism.”

Diversity “across gender expression, across ethnicity and across ages,” she said, “is what makes for a great team,” adding, “It’s about plural thinking, not individual thinking.”

article_text:
One of the old adages of the film business was that people wouldn’t pay to watch an actor in theaters if they could see them for free on TV. Today, AI -generated content in China is ubiquitous, with a recent report suggesting that among the explosion of microdramas in China, nearly two-thirds of those videos are all generated by AI.

But it seems there’s a big difference between what audiences, even Chinese ones, will pay to buy a ticket for compared to what they will consume on their phones for free.

This past weekend, a fully, AI-generated feature film titled “Sanxingdui: Future Past” opened in Chinese theaters and grossed just RMB1.21 million, which is about $181,000, according to the film’s producer Bona Film Group. It’s the first AI feature to get the right to play on Chinese screens, and it makes it a big flop, as Bona in a recent blog post said the budget for the movie was 10 million yuan, which is about $1.5 million.

That’s about the budget of a small indie, and perhaps more than you would’ve guessed when so much of the narrative around AI is that it’s going to cut costs and that you can make “Avatar” for next to nothing. But Bona says the film was produced over the course of two years from a team of 70 to 80 people, and some of the creators bristled at the idea that the images were created with a single click. In fact, the blog post says “Future Past” was being tweaked and technically still “shooting” up until a week before the film hit theaters.

Clearly, though, that level of artistry wasn’t evident on screen. An attendee told the international outlet AFP that the AI still “falls short” of a human-made, live-action production. “In the future, just like films, maybe decades later, it would get to a level when people are all willing to pay to watch,” she told AFP. “But for the moment, I think there would be very few who would.”

Bona had reason to believe that the film could attract a reasonable audience in theaters. “Sanxingdui: Future Past” originated as an AI microdrama series itself that managed nearly 200 million views. In fact, production has already begun on Bona’s second AI-generated feature, “Unplanned Operation in the Cold Moon,” and that the company has received requests to screen the movie in other countries outside of China.

The challenge though of releasing a 100-minute feature compared to a microdrama that could be just a few minutes in length is that it has to go through a content review process before it can be screened in theaters, so that speed to bring something new and fresh to market wasn’t there for “Sanxingdui.”

All of this will be something that the upcoming film from YouTuber and AI creator Gossip Goblin will be watching closely. His fully AI feature, “ Gods Don’t Give Gifts ,” is opening in U.S. theaters this December and is even launching international sales at the American Film Market next month. It’s the first such movie to receive a rating from the MPA, and it’s even intending to submit for eligibility at the Oscars for Best Animated Feature. Gossip Goblin has a large audience that he cultivates across numerous psychedelic, sprawling AI shorts, many of which belong to a connected story universe, so he’s hoping to emulate the Markiplier and “Iron Lung” playbook to draw a dedicated fanbase to theaters via a self-releasing strategy.

But whether it’s in China or America, people go to the theaters expecting a certain level of cinematic quality above what they can get at home on their phones. We’ll see if the “Sanxingdui” experiment ends up translating to American audiences.

In a collection of broken, dog-eared and graffitied books in Bologna, Ilaria Maria Sala finds an antidote to a world being muddled by AI

In early July, right in the middle of Bologna’s university citadel, the new Biblioteca Eco (Eco Library) opened its doors to visitors. The location, at 2 Piazza Puntoni, feels like a tribute: philosopher, novelist and all-round polymath Umberto Eco was born in Alessandria, Piedmont, and passed away in Milan ten years ago, but Bologna is where he lived for more than 45 years, teaching semiotics at university and putting his own signature on the way this subject is viewed. To this day, Bologna and its university are the places with which he is most closely associated. When, in 1971, Italy’s first multidisciplinary undergraduate degree programme opened in Bologna – called DAMS, which stands for Disciplines of the Arts, Music and Drama – Eco was among its cofounders, becoming the chair of the semiotics department in 1975. That programme started a golden era for the city and its university: culture and counterculture seemed to be coexisting in an exciting continuum, unaffected by self-satisfaction. Eco was an embodiment of this openness: his lectures, his articles and, as we can see now, his shelves juxtaposed with pride the latest comics and obscure interpretations of Ancient Latin texts by medieval scholars.

For many, of course, Eco is first and foremost the author of the novel The Name of the Rose , published in 1980 in Italian, and translated worldwide. But what the new Biblioteca Eco puts on show is his wonderfully obsessive relationship with books: loving, compulsive and very physical. As a bibliophile, he was insatiable: more books are in his country house near Urbino, while his ancient volumes collection, mostly on the occult, alchemy, witchcraft and demonology, the sciences and memory techniques, has been bought by the Braidense library, established in Milan by Maria Theresa of Austria in 1770.

The Biblioteca Eco displays, and makes available to the public, a collection of 32,000 volumes, which have been transported here and arranged on the shelves as close as possible to how they were kept in Eco’s last home, in Milan. This has been done through the meticulous, close-to-obsessive work of photographing every millimetre of the original library and then recreating it exactly. The idea is that the visitor and the reader experience as nearly as possible what Eco would have seen when he looked at his shelves. This means that here, unlike in most libraries, books are kept in double rows, in order to make use of the full depth of the shelves, or that they lie on top of other books, precisely as he left them. Inside the books’ pages, too, are all the things that you are not supposed to do to books, which Eco did to books, and defended doing: scribbling notes with an indelible pen, folding the corners of pages into dog ears, opening books flat even at the expense of the spine. And the range of titles included here is as vast as human curiosity: comics, books on games and Dante Alighieri translated in all possible languages. Thrillers, semiotics, philosophy and everything about world religions. Novels and botany. These are books that have been lived in, broken in like a pair of comfortable shoes, roughed up and cuddled. (During my visit, the library’s curators said that the collection provides an excuse for couples to reopen debates about book etiquette: See? He did it too! )

Eco was a defender of owning books, regardless of how many one could actually read, finding that their physical presence, the tactile pleasure of being among them, already initiated a dialogue between the printed pages and their owner. Online there is a short clip of Eco walking at home, as he turns one corner after the other, in a seemingly endless loop of overflowing bookshelves, tables piled high with volumes, more volumes and a few notebooks, and then more bookshelves, opening on more brimming bookshelves.

Paper was everything, even if Eco was fascinated by technology, and used computers and e-readers gladly as acceptable tools. As we increasingly struggle to keep the world of AI distinguishable from the word of reality, the new Biblioteca Eco enters the fray as an amazing antidote to it.

article_text:
One of the highlights of this year’s New York Film Festival is the latest feature by the nonfiction master Gianfranco Rosi, known for documentaries like Sacro GRA (2013), Fire at Sea (2016), and Notturno (2020), which paint both lyrical and urgent portraits of places that function as thresholds—between land and water, life and death, heaven and hell. His new cinematic essay, Below the Clouds , brings that approach to the Italian city of Naples. Shot in ethereal black and white, the film explores Naples as an environment both cosmic and prosaic—a city whose skies are suffused with volcanic ash and whose earth is shaken by tremors; and where a glorious and ancient past scaffolds a gritty, melting-pot present.

Below the Clouds premiered in August at the Venice Film Festival, where Film Comment ‘s Devika Girish sat down with the filmmaker for a conversation. The two discussed how Pietro Marcello (director of the NYFF selection Duse ) inspired Rosi to make a film in Naples, as well as Rosi’s uniquely embedded and immersive technique, and the state of nonfiction cinema today.
